clue.text: Tesla supports US college baseball catcher

indicators.note: in a down entry, what supports something sits beneath it, so this piece comes last

parts.note: the Massachusetts Institute of Technology
T is the symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.surface: An electric-car company sponsors a university's baseball team.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supports' puts the Tesla piece underneath the college.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitt is the padded glove a baseball fielder wears to catch the ball.

clue.text: Bandage decoy plugged by one American's gun

indicators.note: a hole that is plugged has something pushed inside it, so the second part goes into the first

parts.note: a lure is a decoy used to entice
Roman numeral one
gat is old American slang for a pistol

explanation.surface: A decoy dressing is stuffed with an American's firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: A ligature is a cord or thread tied tightly round something, such as a bleeding vessel, so it can serve as a binding or bandage.

clue.text: Cut weightlifting? It's just a question of time

indicators.note: read as weight lifting: in a down entry the letter for weight is raised from the bottom to the top

parts.note: hewn means cut, as with an axe

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether to drop weightlifting, and is told it is only a matter of timing.
explanation.walkthrough: W is the abbreviation for weight; it sits at the foot of HEWN and lifts to the head, giving WHEN.
explanation.definitionFit: When is the interrogative word used to ask about the time at which something happens.

clue.text: Relay rage cost starter in Paris?

indicators.note: read as re-lay: the letters are laid out again in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An angry runner pays the price for losing a relay race in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relay' looks like a race to go with 'starter', but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Snails cooked in garlic butter are a classic French first course, ordered as an hors d'oeuvre in Paris restaurants.

clue.text: Cricket, perhaps, popular with dedicated following

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a sect is a group of devoted adherents

explanation.surface: Cricket is a popular sport with a loyal band of fans.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is the British bat-and-ball game, but here it is the chirping creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket is a jumping, chirping creature with six legs, one example of that class of arthropod.

clue.text: Infernal creatures covering Harry head to toe

indicators.note: the opening letter moves from the head of the string right down to its foot

parts.note: a shell is a protective covering
to harry someone is to hound them

explanation.surface: Something covers young Harry from head to toe, like a blanket.
explanation.walkthrough: Joining the two gives SHELLHOUND; its S then travels from the head to the toe.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellhounds are the demonic dogs of myth that guard or roam the underworld, such as Cerberus.

clue.text: Adopting new top speed, charges hurdles

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so the outer word takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: fees are charges; the word opens around the inserted letters
N is the abbreviation for new
c is the speed of light, the top speed in physics
the rest of the word for charges

explanation.surface: A horse taking on a new top speed charges at the jumps.
explanation.walkthrough: N and C go inside FEES.
explanation.definitionFit: Fences are the obstacles a horse jumps in a steeplechase, the same thing as hurdles.

clue.text: Middle-distance specialist once ran, briefly, in 100m

indicators.note: the shortened word is placed inside the two outer letters
something said briefly is cut short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
taken as written, then shortened
taken as written

explanation.surface: A former middle-distance runner once ran briefly in a 100-metre sprint.
explanation.walkthrough: '100m' looks like the sprint distance; it splits into C and M around the clipped RAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Steve Cram was a British runner of the 1980s who held world records at 1500 metres and the mile.

clue.text: Politician cycling for nation with luck

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective; the people of that nation are proverbially lucky

indicators.note: letters cycling round in order means the last one moves to the front

parts.note: Rishi Sunak, UK Prime Minister 2022 to 2024

explanation.surface: A politician takes up cycling for the good of the country, and gets lucky.
explanation.walkthrough: The final I of RISHI comes round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'the luck of the Irish' attaches good fortune to Ireland's people, so this adjective names that fortunate nation.

clue.text: Writer of poems enters wrestling with one

indicators.note: wrestling twists and contorts, so the letters are wrenched into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet steps into the wrestling ring to take on an opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonneteer composes sonnets, fourteen-line verses, so is a particular kind of poet.

clue.text: Coach just announced price for return?

parts.note: to coach is to train

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so we go by how the word sounds

parts.note: just means fair, which sounds like the word for a ticket price

explanation.surface: A sports coach has just announced the fee for coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' suggests a bus, a neat decoy since the answer is about rail travel. The question mark marks 'return' as a ticket, not a comeback.
explanation.definitionFit: A return is a round-trip ticket, and what you pay for it on the railway is the fare.

clue.text: Substitute, initially left out, controversially undertaking marathon

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of each of the following words

parts.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A stand-in runner, initially left out, controversially takes on a marathon.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a doctor or cleric who temporarily stands in for another, a professional replacement.

clue.text: France due returns in golf and rowing

parts.note: F is the international vehicle code for France

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round
taken as written
golf is G in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: France is due a comeback in golf and rowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' sits beside 'golf' as a sport, but here it is the quarrelling sense, rhyming with 'cowing'.
explanation.definitionFit: To row (rhyming with now) is to quarrel, so rowing and feuding both mean engaged in a bitter dispute.

clue.text: Fighter at amateur boxing won judicial decision

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing in a box, so the outer letters wrap round the next piece

parts.note: F designates a fighter aircraft, as in the F-16
taken as written
W stands for won in sports results tables
A is the abbreviation for amateur

explanation.surface: A fighter at an amateur boxing bout won on the judges' decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing' looks like the sport; it means AT A goes round W.
explanation.definitionFit: A fatwa is a formal legal ruling issued by an Islamic scholar, a judgment on a point of religious law.

clue.text: Iridescent swimming outfit, if revealing, thus described?

definitions.text: Iridescent swimming outfit, if revealing, thus described?

indicators.note: swimming suggests moving about fluidly, so the letters drift into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shimmering swimsuit that shows a lot of skin might be called risqué.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a skimpy, shimmering swimsuit would be called immodest, and that word is the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiscreet means lacking tact or modesty, which fits a swimsuit that reveals too much.

clue.text: Film featuring cross-dressing little piggy

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the 1982 comedy in which Dustin Hoffman's actor poses as a woman
second meaning: a toe, as in the nursery rhyme This Little Piggy

explanation.surface: A film about cross-dressing stars a little pig.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'This little piggy went to market' is counted on a child's toes, hence the childish word for a toe.
explanation.definitionFit: Tootsie is both the title of the Hoffman comedy and a playful word for a toe, which the rhyme calls a piggy.

clue.text: Retired tennis player nevertheless entertains

indicators.note: to entertain is to hold or harbour, so the word holds the answer within it

parts.note: sits inside this word, after its opening N

explanation.surface: A retired tennis star still puts on a show nonetheless.
explanation.definitionFit: Chris Evert is the American tennis champion who won eighteen Grand Slam singles titles before retiring in 1989.

clue.text: Given time, dip into squash

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to dip into a book is to read a bit of it

explanation.surface: Someone with time to spare dips into a game of squash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given' just sets the time piece first; 'squash' is the verb, not the racket sport.
explanation.definitionFit: To tread on something is to press it flat underfoot, a synonym of squash as a verb.

clue.text: Preserve shooting jackets

indicators.note: a jacket wraps round its contents, so the word encloses the answer

parts.note: sits in the middle of this word

explanation.surface: A country estate keeps its tweed shooting jackets in good order.
explanation.definitionFit: To tin food is to seal it in a can so it keeps, one way of preserving it.

clue.text: Exposed state head accepting uniform study

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the outer word receives the rest inside

parts.note: a ness is a headland; it opens around the other letters
uniform is U in the NATO alphabet
a den is a private study
the rest of the word for a headland

explanation.surface: A headmistress is caught out admitting to a study of school uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is a headland here, NESS, as in Loch Ness or Sheerness; U and DEN go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudeness is the condition of being unclothed, a body left exposed.

clue.text: Relative odds cut in mixed crew

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters are cut away, leaving only the even ones

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A relative's chances are slashed in a mixed rowing crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' looks like an anagram signal, but it is part of the string whose even letters are kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is the daughter of one's brother or sister, so a family member.

clue.text: Straight after rejection, tense setter's volcanic

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: straight means undiluted or pure, as of a drink
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
the setter is I, so the setter's (setter has) is I'VE

explanation.surface: A setter, rejected, gets tense and explodes with fury.
explanation.definitionFit: Eruptive describes something that bursts out, as volcanic activity does.

clue.text: Drinking session, having started late, winding up

indicators.note: starting late means missing the beginning, so the first letter is dropped

parts.note: a carousal is a boisterous drinking party

explanation.surface: A drinking session that began late is drawing to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winding up' looks like ending, but it means stirring someone up, the sense that defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Winding someone up provokes or excites them, and arousal is that stirring of feeling.

clue.text: Canoe's breaking lashings

indicators.note: something breaking falls apart, so the letters are scattered into a fresh order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A canoe is breaking up under heavy lashings of rain.
explanation.walkthrough: Lashings is British informal for a great deal, as in 'lashings of cream'.
explanation.definitionFit: Oceans is informal for a vast quantity, so it matches lashings meaning plenty.

clue.text: Party missing volleyball getting lost in Nice

indicators.note: letters that get lost wander off course and end up rearranged
missing means lacking, so the word for a party is taken away

parts.note: a ball is a formal dancing party
taken as written

explanation.surface: A beach party with no volleyball leaves someone at a loose end in Nice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' is capitalised as the French resort but means pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovely and nice are both everyday words for pleasing or delightful.

clue.text: Discus half completed — right before shot put upset

indicators.note: before means placed ahead of what follows in the answer
only half of the word is finished, so the back half is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, then halved

indicators.note: shot means ruined or wrecked, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A field athlete leaves the discus half done and goes straight to the shot put.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot put' looks like the athletics event; 'shot' is the signal and 'put' is the letters it scrambles.
explanation.definitionFit: To disrupt something is to throw it into disorder, which is one sense of the verb upset.

clue.text: One escaping hammer freely released at last

indicators.note: to hammer is to beat out of shape, so the letters are battered into a new order
the last letter is let go, so it falls off the end

parts.note: taken as written, then trimmed

explanation.surface: A prisoner on the run, finally freed, swings a hammer.
explanation.walkthrough: With the companion clues, 'hammer' and 'discus' make an athletics theme; here 'hammer' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleer is someone who flees, a person running away from danger or capture.

clue.text: Start off football downcast, dropping left winger

indicators.note: in a down entry the letter for left drops from the top to the bottom
the start of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: opening letter
downcast means low in spirits

explanation.surface: A footballer, feeling low after being dropped, is the team's left winger.
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for left; it moves from the top of LOW to the foot. 'Winger' looks like a football position but means anything with wings.
explanation.definitionFit: Fowl are birds, and a bird is a creature with wings, hence a winger in crossword wit.

clue.text: Admired victor made grand exits

indicators.note: one letter leaves its place and the new letter fills the gap it left

parts.note: victor is V in the NATO alphabet
to generate something is to make it
G stands for grand, slang for a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A winner who made a thousand pounds makes a grand exit and is much admired.
explanation.walkthrough: G leaves the front of GENERATED and V takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: To venerate someone is to regard them with deep respect, so venerated means highly admired.

clue.text: Stay one off the front in steeplechase?

indicators.note: a single letter is removed from the front of the word

parts.note: a brace is a stay or support

explanation.surface: A rider stays on, one fence from the front, in the steeplechase.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeplechase is one kind of contest of speed, over fences on horseback or barriers on a track.

clue.text: Hard bugger climbing for money

indicators.note: climbing goes upward, so in a down entry the letters are read from the bottom

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
sod is a mild British insult for an annoying person

explanation.surface: A tough so-and-so climbs the ladder for cash.
explanation.walkthrough: Dosh is British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Dosh is informal British slang for cash, so it means money.

clue.text: Carol's Bohemian — a good looker?

parts.note: surface: a woman called Carol has a free-spirited, arty partner
setter's reading: the Christmas carol's Bohemian duke, a good king who looked out on the Feast of Stephen

explanation.surface: Carol's bohemian boyfriend is rather handsome.
explanation.walkthrough: The carol opens 'Good King Wenceslas looked out', so he is good and a looker; he was a duke of Bohemia.
explanation.definitionFit: The tenth-century saint and Duke of Bohemia is the hero of a Christmas carol in which he looks out on the snow.

clue.text: Gentlemen head for sailing on bay

indicators.note: in an across entry, on means placed after

parts.note: a cove is a small bay

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: opening letter

explanation.surface: Gentlemen set out on a sailing trip across the bay.
explanation.walkthrough: Cove is old British slang for a man or fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Coves is dated British slang for men or chaps, so it can stand for gentlemen.
